title: ITN 170 Final Exam Review
description: A review of everything on the instructor's final study guide: navigation, file maintenance, permissions, wildcards, viewing files, monitoring, processes and services, finding files and links, redirection and the text tools, users and sudo, vi, cron and shell scripting.

questions.question: Match each navigation command to what it does.

pairs.right: List the files in a directory
Show the account you are logged in as
Display the manual page for a command

questions.question: What is the difference between `cd ..` and `cd .`?
options: `cd ..` moves up to the parent directory; `cd .` stays in the current directory
`cd ..` moves to the home directory; `cd .` moves to the root directory
`cd ..` moves down into the first subdirectory; `cd .` moves up one level
They are identical; both go to the parent directory
questions.explanation: A single dot is the current directory and two dots are its parent, so `cd .` does nothing visible and `cd ..` goes up one level.

questions.question: What does `pwd` stand for?
questions.explanation: pwd prints the full path of the directory you are currently in.

questions.question: Which command shows the account you are currently logged in to the shell as?
questions.explanation: `whoami` prints just your user name. `who` is a different command: it lists everyone logged in.

questions.question: What does `su -` do when run without a user name?
options: Shows a list of all users
Switches back to the previous directory
Runs one command with root privileges and then returns
Switches to the root user (su stands for switch user), after asking for root's password
questions.explanation: `su` with no user name means root. The dash gives you root's full login environment. `sudo` is the one that runs a single command with elevated rights.

questions.question: What does `sudo` do?
options: Lets a permitted user run a command with root (superuser) privileges
Permanently turns your account into root
Switches the shell to a different directory
questions.explanation: sudo runs one command with root privileges, after checking you are allowed to. `sudo su` uses that permission to start a root shell.

questions.question: What does `ls -ltr` show?
options: A long listing sorted alphabetically in reverse
A long listing sorted by modification time, oldest first (newest last)
Only the files owned by root
A recursive listing of every subdirectory
questions.explanation: `-l` is the long format, `-t` sorts by modification time (newest first) and `-r` reverses that order. Compare plain `ls`, which gives names only, and `ls -l`, which adds permissions, owner, size and date.

questions.question: Which command clears the terminal screen?
questions.explanation: `clear` wipes the visible screen (Ctrl+L does the same).

questions.question: Which command searches a file for a pattern or string?
questions.explanation: grep prints the lines of a file that match a pattern. `find` searches for files by name or attribute, not by content.

questions.question: List the files in ~/labs/links in a long listing, with the oldest at the top and the newest at the bottom.
questions.explanation: -l long format, -t sort by time, -r reverse so the newest comes last.

questions.question: Print the full path of the directory you are in right now.
questions.explanation: `pwd` prints the current working directory. A fresh terminal starts in your home directory.

questions.question: Match each file maintenance command to what it does.

pairs.right: Deletes a directory and its contents

questions.question: Which command renames a file?
questions.explanation: `mv oldname newname` renames. The same command moves a file when the destination is another directory.

questions.question: What happens if you run `rmdir` on a directory that still contains files?
options: It fails with an error; rmdir only removes empty directories
It deletes the directory and everything inside it
It deletes only the files, leaving the directory
It asks for confirmation and then deletes everything
questions.explanation: rmdir refuses to remove a non-empty directory. To remove a directory and its contents you need `rm -r`.

questions.question: What does `rm -Rf` do?
options: Renames a file and forces the new name
Forcefully removes a directory, all of its subdirectories and their contents, without prompting
Lists what would be deleted without deleting it
questions.explanation: -R (or -r) means recursive, -f means force (no prompts, ignore missing files). It is the most dangerous command on this list, so double-check the path.

questions.question: Match each command that changes a file's properties to what it changes.
In ~/labs/files, make a copy of notes.txt called notes-copy.txt.
questions.explanation: cp source destination leaves the original in place.

questions.question: In ~/labs/files, rename report1.txt to report-final.txt.
questions.explanation: mv with a destination in the same directory is a rename.

questions.question: Create a new directory named ~/labs/archive-2025.
questions.explanation: mkdir creates the directory.

questions.question: In ~/labs/files, delete the directory old together with everything inside it.
questions.explanation: rmdir would refuse because old is not empty; rm -r removes the directory and its contents.

questions.question: Create an empty file named ~/labs/newfile.txt.
questions.explanation: touch creates an empty file if it does not exist (and updates the timestamp if it does).

questions.question: What number does each permission have in octal (numeric) mode?
questions.explanation: Add the values for each of owner, group and other: rwx = 4+2+1 = 7, r-x = 5, r-- = 4.

questions.question: Which permissions does `chmod 755 file` set?
questions.explanation: 7 = rwx for the owner, 5 = r-x for the group, 5 = r-x for others.

questions.question: Which permissions does `chmod 644 file` set?
questions.explanation: 6 = rw- for the owner, 4 = r-- for the group and for others. It is the usual mode for an ordinary file.

questions.question: Which octal mode makes a file readable and writable by its owner only?
questions.explanation: 600 is rw-------. 700 would also grant execute.

questions.question: Which octal mode matches `rwxr-x---`?
What does `chown alice:staff report.txt` do?
options: Gives alice and staff read access
Copies report.txt to alice's home directory
Makes alice the owner and staff the owning group of report.txt
questions.explanation: chown changes ownership; the part after the colon is the group. `chgrp staff report.txt` would change only the group.

questions.question: To run a script as `./myscript`, which permission does it need?
options: Execute (and read, since the shell has to read a script)
questions.explanation: Running it with `bash myscript` instead needs only read permission, because bash opens the file rather than executing it.

questions.question: Make ~/labs/perms/team.txt readable, writable and executable by its owner, readable and executable by its group, and not accessible at all to others.
Make ~/labs/perms/noexec.sh executable by its owner, adding no other permissions to any set.
questions.explanation: Symbolic mode: u = user (owner), + adds, x = execute. It leaves every other bit alone.

questions.question: `touch project{1..4} project{12..14} project{a,e,g,h}` creates how many files?
questions.explanation: Brace expansion runs before the command: {1..4} gives 4 names, {12..14} gives 3 and {a,e,g,h} gives 4. 4 + 3 + 4 = 11.

questions.question: In `ls project*`, what does the `*` match?
questions.explanation: `*` matches any run of characters, including none, so plain `project` is listed too.

questions.question: In `ls project?`, what does the `?` match?
questions.explanation: `?` is a single-character wildcard.

questions.question: A directory holds project, project1-4, project12-14 and projecta, projecte, projectg, projecth. Which files does `ls project??` list?
options: Every file whose name starts with project
questions.explanation: Two question marks mean exactly two characters after `project`.

questions.question: A directory holds project, project1-4, project12-14 and projecta, projecte, projectg, projecth. Which files does `ls project[13]?` list?
questions.explanation: The first character after `project` must be 1 or 3, then exactly one more character. That matches project12, project13 and project14 (project1 has no second character).

questions.question: A directory holds project, project1-4, project12-14 and projecta, projecte, projectg, projecth. Which files does `ls project[aegh]` list?
options: None; brackets do not work in file names
questions.explanation: A bracket matches exactly one character from the set. `project[a-h]` would match the same four files, as a-h is a range.

questions.question: What does `ls project[!135]` match?
options: The files project1, project3 and project5 only
Names with no characters after project
A name starting with project followed by one character that is not 1, 3 or 5
questions.explanation: Inside brackets, `!` negates the set.

questions.question: In ~/wild, list only the files whose name is `project` followed by exactly one digit.
questions.hint: Use a range inside square brackets.
questions.explanation: A bracket range of [0-9] matches one digit. (`project?` would also pick up projecta, projecte and so on.)

questions.question: In ~/wild, list the files named project followed by one character that is not 1, 3 or 5.
questions.explanation: `[!135]` is one character that is not 1, 3 or 5.

questions.question: In ~/wild, list the files named projecta, projecte, projectg and projecth, using a range of letters.
questions.explanation: `[a-h]` matches one character from a to h.

questions.question: Match each file display command to what it does.

pairs.right: Shows a file's contents on the screen
Shows a file's contents in reverse order, last line first
Shows a file one page at a time
Shows a file one page at a time, and lets you scroll backwards
Shows the first lines of a file
Shows the last lines of a file

questions.question: By default, how many lines do `head` and `tail` show?
questions.explanation: Use -n to change it, for example `tail -n 3 file`.

questions.question: Which command shows a file with its last line first?
questions.explanation: tac is cat spelled backwards, and it prints the lines backwards.

questions.question: While viewing a file in `less`, which key scrolls forward one line at a time?
questions.explanation: `j` goes down a line (and `k` up), and `q` quits.

questions.question: Which of these pairs are text editors?
questions.explanation: vi and nano both create and edit files. The others only display them.

questions.question: Show only the last 3 lines of ~/labs/text/fruit.txt.
questions.explanation: `tail -n 3` (or `tail -3`).

questions.question: Show the first 2 lines of ~/labs/text/numbers.txt.
questions.explanation: `head -n 2` (or `head -2`).

questions.question: Print the contents of ~/labs/text/numbers.txt in reverse line order.
questions.explanation: tac prints the last line first.

questions.question: Match each user-monitoring command to what it shows.

pairs.right: Who is logged in and what each of them is doing
Your user ID, group ID and group memberships
A summary of each user, including idle time and login time

questions.question: Match each system utility to what it does.

pairs.right: Shows how long the system has been running
Shows the kernel and operating system type
Shows where a command is located

questions.question: Which command shows the full path of a program, for example `/usr/bin/pwd` for `pwd`?
questions.explanation: `which pwd` searches the directories in your PATH and prints the first match.

questions.question: What does `cal 9 2016` display?
questions.explanation: `cal month year`; with only a year, as in `cal 2016`, it shows all twelve months.

questions.question: Which command tells you how long the system has been running?
questions.explanation: uptime also shows the number of logged-in users and the load average.

questions.question: Which command shows the Linux kernel release, for example 5.14.0?
questions.explanation: `uname` alone prints the OS type (Linux); `-r` adds the kernel release, and `-a` shows everything.

questions.question: Display the name of this machine.
questions.explanation: `hostname` prints the system's host name.

questions.question: Display the kernel release of this machine.
questions.explanation: `uname -r` prints the kernel release.

questions.question: Display your user ID, group ID and the groups you belong to.
questions.explanation: `id` shows uid, gid and all group memberships.

questions.question: Match each command to what it does.

pairs.right: Lists processes running on the system
Shows running processes with live CPU and memory use
Terminates a process by its process ID
Shows free disk space for each file system
Prints kernel messages, such as hardware warnings and errors
Shows network connections, routing and interface information

questions.question: Which command replaced `service` for starting and stopping services in RHEL 7 and later?
questions.explanation: systemctl controls systemd services, for example `systemctl start httpd`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `systemctl start httpd` and `systemctl enable httpd`?
options: start runs the service now; enable makes it start automatically at boot
start runs it at boot; enable runs it now
enable installs the package; start removes it
questions.explanation: To do both at once: `systemctl enable --now httpd`.

questions.question: What does `iostat 1` do?
options: Prints one line of statistics and exits
Prints input/output statistics and refreshes them every second
Limits disk I/O to 1 MB per second
questions.explanation: The number is the interval in seconds between reports.

questions.question: Which file under /proc contains information about the CPU?
questions.explanation: `cat /proc/cpuinfo`. For memory, read /proc/meminfo.

questions.question: Which file under /proc contains information about memory?
questions.explanation: `cat /proc/meminfo`.

questions.question: Which command gives you your disk partition information and usage?
questions.explanation: `df -h` shows sizes in human-readable units. `free` is for RAM, not disks.

questions.question: `top` shows all running processes together with their resource usage, and updates the display continuously.
questions.explanation: Press q to quit.

questions.question: An ordinary user, with no extra privilege, can start and stop any system service and kill any process.
questions.explanation: Starting and stopping system services requires root (for example via sudo), and an ordinary user can only kill their own processes.

questions.question: Show the free and used memory in human-readable units.
questions.explanation: -h gives GiB/MiB instead of raw KiB.

questions.question: Show the disk space used by each file system in human-readable units.
questions.explanation: -h gives sizes like 19G instead of 1K-blocks.

questions.question: Which command searches the current directory and all subdirectories for a file named mike?
questions.explanation: The first argument to find is where to start; `.` means the current directory, `/` would search the whole system.

questions.question: Which command searches the whole system for a file named ifcfg-enp0s3?
questions.explanation: Starting from `/` covers the entire file system; run it with sudo to avoid permission errors.

questions.question: Which command finds a file by name quickly by looking it up in a prebuilt database, for example `___ mike`?
questions.explanation: `locate` is fast but only as current as its database, which `updatedb` refreshes. `find` walks the real directories each time.

questions.question: How does `locate` differ from `find`?
options: locate searches file contents; find searches names
locate searches a prebuilt database (fast, may be out of date); find searches the live file system
locate only works as root; find works for everyone
questions.explanation: A file created a minute ago will not show up in `locate` until `updatedb` runs.

questions.question: What happens to a soft (symbolic) link if the original file is deleted or renamed?
options: The link is turned into a regular file
The link breaks and points at nothing
questions.explanation: A soft link stores the original's name, like a shortcut in Windows. A hard link is another name for the same data, so deleting, renaming or moving the original does not affect it.

questions.question: What happens to a hard link if the original file is deleted, renamed or moved?
options: It keeps working; the data remains as long as one name exists
questions.explanation: Hard links are extra names for the same inode.

questions.question: Match each command to the link it creates.
In ~/labs/links, create a soft link named shortcut.txt that points to original.txt.
questions.explanation: `ln -s target linkname` makes a symbolic link; `ls -l` shows it with an arrow.

questions.question: In ~/labs/links, create a hard link named backup.txt for original.txt.
questions.explanation: Without -s, ln makes a hard link. Afterwards, the file's link count goes up.

questions.question: Find every file named notes.txt under ~/labs/files.
questions.explanation: The path is where to start; -name is the filename pattern.

questions.question: What is the difference between `ls -ltr > filename` and `ls -ltr >> filename`?
options: `>` writes (overwriting the file); `>>` appends to the end of the file
questions.explanation: Use `>` with care: it replaces whatever was in the file.

questions.question: What does a pipe (`|`) do?
options: Sends the output of one command to the input of the next
Runs two commands at the same time and ignores their output
Runs the second command only if the first fails
questions.explanation: For example `ls -l /etc | more`.

questions.question: What does `ls -l | head` show?
options: The last 10 lines of the long listing
The first 10 lines of the long listing
questions.explanation: `tail` would show the last 10 instead.

questions.question: Match each text tool to what it does.

pairs.right: Searches for lines matching a pattern
Collapses repeated adjacent lines (and counts them with -c)
Processes text field by field, for example printing one column
Edits a stream of text, for example substituting one string for another
Writes its input to a file and also to the screen

questions.question: Why does `uniq` normally need `sort` first?
options: uniq cannot read a file without being sorted
sort converts the file to a format uniq understands
uniq only removes duplicates that are next to each other
questions.explanation: That is why `sort file | uniq -c` is the standard counting pipeline.

questions.question: The file `animals` has two columns, a name and a type, such as `Tiger Cat`. Which pipeline counts how many lines there are of each type?
questions.explanation: awk prints the second field, sort groups identical types together, and uniq -c counts each group.

questions.question: Append the text second to the end of ~/log.txt without deleting what is already there.
questions.explanation: `>>` appends; `>` would overwrite the file.

questions.question: Match each account-management command to what it does.

pairs.right: Sets or changes a user's password
Switches to another user's login session

questions.question: Which command adds the existing user newuser to the wheel group so they can use sudo, without removing them from other groups?
questions.explanation: -G sets the supplementary groups and -a appends. Without -a, usermod replaces all of the user's supplementary groups, silently removing them from every other group.

questions.question: On CentOS and RHEL, the members of which special group are allowed to run all commands as root through sudo?
questions.explanation: Members of wheel are granted full sudo access by the default /etc/sudoers file. On Debian and Ubuntu the equivalent is called sudo.

questions.question: What does the `wheel` group allow its members to do?
options: Run any command as root with sudo
questions.explanation: The group name is just a label; the line `%wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL` in sudoers is what gives it power.

questions.question: A normal user runs `ls -la /root/` and gets `Permission denied`. What do they run to get the listing?
questions.explanation: sudo runs just that one command as root.

questions.question: When a wheel member runs a command with sudo, whose password is requested?
questions.explanation: sudo checks that you are allowed to, using your own credentials; that is why you don't need to share root's password.

questions.question: A new sudo user runs `sudo whoami`. What is printed?
questions.explanation: The command ran as root, so `whoami` reports root.

questions.question: After creating a user with `adduser newuser`, what must you do before they can log in?
options: Add them to the wheel group
questions.explanation: A new account is locked until a password is set. Passwords failing the dictionary check will be rejected for being weak.

questions.question: `sudo su` switches you to the root user.
questions.explanation: `sudo su` uses sudo to run `su`, which starts a root shell. `sudo -i` is the usual way to do the same thing.

questions.question: What does `su - newuser` do?
options: Runs the next command as newuser, then returns
Switches to newuser with a full login environment (requires newuser's password unless you are root)
questions.explanation: Use `exit` to return to the previous user.

questions.question: Create a new user account named carol.
questions.explanation: `useradd` creates the account; use sudo as an ordinary user.

questions.question: Create a new group named developers.
questions.explanation: `groupadd` creates a group.

questions.question: The user bob already exists. Add bob to the wheel group, keeping any groups he is already in.
questions.explanation: -a (append) must go with -G, or bob's other groups would be replaced.

questions.question: Match each vi key or command to what it does.

pairs.right: Leave insert mode and return to command mode
Replace the character under the cursor
Delete the character under the cursor

questions.question: You made changes you don't want to keep. Which command leaves vi without saving?
questions.explanation: The `!` forces the quit even though the buffer has unsaved changes.

questions.question: Which of these saves your changes and quits vi?
questions.explanation: :wq and :x do the same. ZZ only works from command mode.

questions.question: You open a file in vi and start typing, but nothing appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: You are in command mode; press i to enter insert mode first
questions.explanation: vi starts in command mode, where keys are commands rather than text.

questions.question: In command mode, how do you search for the word error?
questions.explanation: Press n for the next match.

questions.question: Which key do you press to leave insert mode and return to command mode?
questions.explanation: Esc is the way out of any mode.

questions.question: What are the five time fields of a crontab entry, in order?
options: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
hour, minute, day of week, day of month, month
questions.explanation: Then comes the command to run. `*` means every value.

questions.question: Match each crontab option to what it does.

pairs.right: Edit your cron jobs (opens an editor, vi by default)

questions.question: What does the entry `0 3 * * * /root/Backup.sh` do?
options: Runs it at 3 p.m. on the first of each month
Runs it three times a day
questions.explanation: Minute 0, hour 3, any day, any month, any weekday.

questions.question: What does the entry `30 16 2 * * /path/to/script.sh` do?
options: Runs it at 4:30 a.m. every day
Runs the script at 4:30 p.m. on the 2nd of every month
Runs it every 30 minutes on the 2nd
questions.explanation: A crontab line has five time fields, so minute 30, hour 16 (24-hour clock), day of month 2.

questions.question: What does the entry `0 22 * * 1-5 /scripts/phpscripts.sh` do?
options: Runs it at 10:00 p.m. on the 1st to 5th of each month
Runs it every day at 1:05 a.m.
Runs it at 10:00 a.m. on weekends
Runs the script at 10:00 p.m., Monday to Friday
questions.explanation: The fifth field is the day of the week; 1-5 is Monday through Friday.

questions.question: What does the entry `*/30 * * * * /path/to/script` do?
options: Runs it once at 30 minutes past midnight
Runs it 30 times per day, at random
questions.explanation: `*/n` means every n units of that field.

questions.question: What does the entry `5 4 * * sun /path/to/linuxcommand` do?
options: Runs the command at 04:05 every Sunday
Runs it at 04:05 every day for a month
Runs it at 4:05 p.m. on Sunday
questions.explanation: Day names can be used in the day-of-week field.

questions.question: What does the entry `23 0-23/2 * * * /path/to/script.sh` do?
options: Runs it at 11:00 p.m. every 2 days
Runs the script at 23 minutes past every second hour (00:23, 02:23, 04:23...)
questions.explanation: The hour field `0-23/2` means every second hour from 0 through 23.

questions.question: What does the entry `22 20 * 3 * command` do?
options: Runs it at 22:20 on the 3rd of every month
Runs it at 8:22 p.m. on March 3 only
Runs it every 22 minutes in March
Runs the command at 8:22 p.m. every day in March
questions.explanation: Minute 22, hour 20, any day of month, month 3, any weekday.

questions.question: Which crontab entry runs /home/user/cleanup.sh at 6:15 a.m. every Monday?
questions.explanation: Minute first, then hour; the last field is the day of week (1 = Monday). The third field is the day of the *month*.

questions.question: Match each cron shortcut to when it runs.
Which is the same as `@daily`?
questions.explanation: @midnight and @daily are synonyms; @annually and @yearly are likewise.

questions.question: In the class exercise, why was the system clock set with `date -s` as root before editing the crontab?
options: Because cron refuses to run unless the date has been set
Because crontab -e needs the clock to be in 2023
So the job's scheduled time was only a minute or two away and the job could be seen running
To log the job's output to a file
questions.explanation: Setting the clock close to the scheduled time avoids waiting a full day to see the job run.

questions.question: What is the first line `#!/bin/bash` of a script called, and what does it do?
options: The header that sets the script's permissions
The line that gives the script its name
The shebang (hashbang); it names the interpreter that runs the script
questions.explanation: The kernel reads it to find which program should run the file.

questions.question: Any command you can type at the bash prompt can also be put in a shell script.
questions.explanation: A script is a sequence of commands that bash runs in order.

questions.question: Which two ways of running a script are correct?
options: `bash myscript` and `./myscript` (the latter needs execute permission)
questions.explanation: `bash myscript` needs only read permission. `./myscript` requires `chmod +x myscript` first.

questions.question: Which is a correct `if` statement in bash?
questions.explanation: Spaces inside the brackets are required, and the block is closed with `fi` (if backwards).

questions.question: What does `for i in 1 2 3; do echo $i; done` print?
options: 1, then 2, then 3, each on its own line
questions.explanation: The loop runs once for each value, setting i each time.

questions.question: How is a `case` statement closed?
questions.explanation: Each pattern's commands end with `;;`. `fi` closes an if and `done` closes a loop.

questions.question: Using a for loop, print the lines `Number 1`, `Number 2` and `Number 3`.
questions.solution: for i in 1 2 3; do echo "Number $i"; done
questions.explanation: The loop variable is set to each value in turn.

questions.question: Write a short bash script that prints `Hello, <name>` for each of the names alice, bob and carol, using a for loop. Include the first line that tells the system which shell runs it.
questions.modelAnswer:
#!/bin/bash
for name in alice bob carol
do
  echo "Hello, $name"
done
rubric: Uses a for loop over the three names (for name in alice bob carol; do ... done)
Prints each name with echo and refers to the loop variable with $
questions.explanation: To run it you would save it as hello.sh, `chmod +x hello.sh` and run `./hello.sh`.

questions.question: Explain the steps to create a user named alice and give her the ability to run commands as root with sudo, naming the command for each step.
questions.modelAnswer:
1. Switch to root or use sudo: `sudo su`.
2. Create the account: `useradd alice` (or `adduser alice`).
3. Set a password: `passwd alice`.
4. Add her to the wheel group: `usermod -aG wheel alice` - the -a is essential so her other groups are kept.
5. Test: `su - alice`, then `sudo whoami` should print root.
rubric: Creates the user with useradd or adduser
Adds the user to the wheel group using usermod -aG (with -a to append)
Describes testing with su - and sudo (for example sudo whoami returning root)
questions.explanation: This is the sudoers how-to from class: create the user, set a password, add to wheel, test.
